newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Mallinckrodt says can handle big debtload.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mallinckrodt says can handle big debtload.

text.p: Medical company Mallinckrodt Inc. tried to assure investors Thursday it will work quickly to reduce the massive debt that will accompany its planned $1.9 billion acquisition of Nellcor Puritan Bennett Inc.
Mallinckrodt Chief Executive Officer Raymond Holman acknowledged the high debt load could be risky, but said the deal is key to its goal of expanding in the health care industry.

The company also said the acquisition of the medical device company will dilute earnings by 15 percent in its current fiscal year ending in June, but boost results by 10 percent to 15 percent in the following year. It also said it intends to take a one-time charge of $325 million to $600 million against earnings in the current year.
Despite the assurances, Wall Street focused on the risks associated with high debt levels resulting from the company's biggest-ever transaction.
"The debt level does add financial risk to the integration level," said Gary Stevenson of A.G. Edwards.

The transaction will send the company's debt soaring to 70 percent of capital from the company's traditional level of 50 percent. The company recently used cash generated from two divestitures to reduce debt to current level of 35 percent to capital.

The $1.9 billion deal announced late Wednesday relies on a $1.2 billion credit line secured by the company, as well as $700 million in cash on hand. The transaction calls for Mallinckrodt to pay $28.50 per share for Nellcor.

"We're a financially conservative company, so any time we get to that level, it's a concern. While the level is high at 70 percent, I think we can work it down fairly expeditiously," Holman said in an interview.
He also said the financial success of the transaction will be based on cost savings, not growth.
The rising debt prompted Standard & Poor's to sound an alarm about the company, placing it on negative CreditWatch and saying that a downgrade would likely follow.
Holman said he was not surprised by the move, noting that company officials were meeting with the rating agencies Thursday to discuss the transaction.
Based in St. Louis, Mallinckrodt recently sold its animal health and flavorings business in order to focus on three areas: respiratory products, medical imaging and specialty pharmaceuticals.
Pleasanton, Calif.-based Nellcor specializes in respiratory medical devices such as oxygen monitors and ventilators for homes, hospitals and nursing facilities.
"This is not just an evolution for Mallinckrodt. It enables us to complete our transformation," Holman said, noting that the two companies had been discussing merger plans for months.
He also said the acquisition of Nellcor will make Mallinckrodt less dependent on the medical imaging business, which recently has suffered from weak pricing.
Mallinckrodt stock lost $1.50 to $38.25 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Nellcor Puritan stock soared $7.15625 to $28.09375 on Nasdaq.
Holman also said the companies do not expect any antitrust issues to block the transaction.
"There is virtually no competition between the two companies," he said, adding that the product lines are complementary but do not overlap.
The combined company will have sales of about $2.4 billion.
